title: Most Young Children on SDF-First Caries Pathway Avoided General Anesthesia
html:
Most young children whose caries management began with 38% silver diamine fluoride were treated without dental general anesthesia over about two years, according to a retrospective cohort study published Nov. 14 in Clinical Oral Investigations.

The study reviewed records of children ages 1 to 8 who received SDF at a German university dental center in 2019 and 2020. All had a high caries burden, limited cooperation with invasive chairside treatment, or both. The 52 children had a mean age of 4.0 years and a mean dmft of 7.8, and 304 primary teeth with ICDAS 3–5 lesions were treated with SDF.

After a mean follow-up of 23.4 months, 46 of the 52 children, or 88.5%, had been managed without dental general anesthesia. Six children, or 11.5%, underwent treatment under general anesthesia.

At the tooth level, 273 teeth, or 89.8%, remained clinically successful, while 31 teeth, or 10.2%, developed a major failure, defined as irreversible pulpitis or abscess. No minor failures were documented. Of the teeth without major failure, 165 received no further restorative treatment, and 108 received minimally invasive restorations as part of the staged pathway.

The authors said initial caries stabilization with SDF may allow time for a child’s cooperation to improve, so that later restorative treatment can be performed without general anesthesia.

The study was conducted by Ruba Abdulrahim, Ruth M. Santamaría, Christian H. Splieth, and colleagues in the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at University Medicine Greifswald in Germany. The authors declared no competing interests.

The study had no comparison group, so it cannot show how much of the favorable outcome is attributable to SDF itself. The authors called for comparative prospective studies to determine SDF’s specific contribution.

Sources:
Clinical Oral Investigations, “Effect of minimally invasive caries management with silver diammine fluoride on caries progression and subsequent need for dental general anaesthesia in children: a retrospective cohort study,” published online Nov. 14, 2026: link.springer.com/10.1007/s00784-026-07277-w
